title: I support my parents and want my own space. Should I buy at auction?
excerpt: A single man earning RM15,000 on contract pays for a semi-D his parents live in and wants to buy an auction unit for himself. Sean steers him away from auctions and suggests moving out first.

question.asker: From Dean, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Dean is single and works in KL city centre on a contract paying about RM15,000 a month. He owns a RM500,000 semi-detached house in the Klang Valley with an instalment of about RM2,300, but his parents and grandmother live there and he has only a small room. He spends about RM4,000 a month on them, including the instalment, their insurance, car and utilities, and has saved RM200,000.
question.text: He plans to buy an auction unit of about RM500,000 near public transport next year to live in or rent out. Is that the right move?

answer.quote: Treat the house as the last obligation of love.
answer.summary: Keep supporting the house, but don't make an auction unit your next step. Either talk openly with his parents about a smaller home, or simply move out to a rented place near the city, keep the RM200,000 as a safety net, and buy an investment through a lower-capital channel.

reasons.title: Auctions often close at market price
reasons.body: Listings start about 30% below valuation, but a few eager bidders push the final price to around or above market. You can't view the unit, and outstanding maintenance, private caveats or a poor as-is condition can surface after you have paid the deposit.

reasons.title: A deadline can burn the deposit
reasons.body: If you can't sign the final agreement within the set period, about 30 days, the deposit is forfeited. Sean, who has bought new, subsale and through investment clubs, still avoids auctions.

reasons.title: His risk is higher than most
reasons.body: If a wrong investment coincides with losing his contract job, his parents and grandmother could lose their home. He needs income of about three times the instalment, roughly RM8,000, just to keep the house safe.

reasons.title: Two or three properties are enough
reasons.body: Sean's aim for viewers is two to three properties in a lifetime, about one every ten years. Bought at RM400,000 to RM600,000 and paid off by 77, they are worth about RM1.5 million in today's money, so you don't become a burden on your own children.

actions: If your family can talk about money, discuss your parents moving to a smaller rented terrace while you keep giving the same monthly sum.
Otherwise rent a room or small unit nearer the city for privacy and career, and visit your parents every week or two.
Keep the RM200,000 split between an emergency fund for your parents, your wedding and renovation, rather than spending it on a purchase.
Compare all four buying channels; a subsale needs about 17% to 18% of the price upfront, about RM90,000 for a RM500,000 unit.
Consider an investment unit under construction bought through a bulk-purchase club, which needs less capital and gives you two to three years before handover.
caveat: Auctions can suit an experienced investor on a third or fourth property who knows the traps. Sean's advice on moving out depends on the family: in many Asian households asking parents to move is a sensitive step.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #255, sponsored by PropertyGuru's Brickz transaction reports. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in June 2024. Sean says his last three purchases came through the bulk-purchase investment club linked in his video description.
